narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 78% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission, this probability led to your application being rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. While accepted students typically rank around the middle of their class, you placed in the bottom decile. Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also increased the likelihood of failure. At 26, it sits well below the average of 37 among students who were admitted. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important feature, but it worked in the opposite direction, slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure. Even so, a 2.1 GPA is noticeably below the 3.23 average of accepted students and could not offset the other signals.

Your part-time study plans, family income in the middle bracket, gender, and race played no role in this outcome, as the model did not consider them.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class ranking through consistent high performance in the remaining law school years and consider retaking the LSAT to bring your score closer to the level of admitted students. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction. (218 words)
